MF-DRO · research progress · 27 Aug 2026

Why MF-DRO Loses

One hundred runs across five methods and four benchmarks settled the headline question negatively: MF-DRO beat no baseline anywhere. Diagnosing why produced a fix that appeared to clear that bar on one benchmark — and a clean re-test at fresh seeds withdrew it. The original finding stands.

h83 · 100/100 runs · 0 failures ROI experiment complete · 34/34 5 seeds · cost 200 post-init

Retraction · announced, then withdrawn

The Hartmann result did not replicate

An earlier version of this page reported that a calibrated Region of Interest moved MF-DRO past the best baseline on Hartmann, overturning the headline above. A clean re-test — the ROI setting fixed in advance, a single arm, five seeds never used before, and the analysis script committed before the runs finished — failed to reproduce it: 2 of 5 seeds, against a bar requiring 4. The claim is withdrawn, and this retraction is given the same prominence the claim was.

seedMF-DRO + ROIMF-MESdifference
472.190.37+1.82
484.6610.68−6.01
499.5625.25−15.69
507.957.20+0.74
516.985.95+1.03

Why the earlier number was misleading. The average difference across these five seeds still favours MF-DRO by 3.62 points — and that average is almost entirely one seed. On seed 49 the baseline collapses (25.25%) and MF-DRO does not (9.56%). On three of the other four, MF-DRO loses, by 0.74, 1.03 and 1.82. The honest description is that it wins big when the baseline happens to fail and loses narrowly the rest of the time.

A follow-up test removed the consolation. That pattern was described as “lower tail risk rather than better typical performance”. Checked across every benchmark and both seed sets, it does not hold: MF-DRO has the smaller worst case on only two of five, and on two benchmarks it has both a wider spread and a worse tail than the baseline. The pattern belongs to the five seeds that produced it, not to the method. An earlier attempt to test it by correlating the baseline’s regret against the difference was itself invalid — that correlation is negative by construction, since both terms share the baseline.

This is precisely why the original comparison required both a lower average and a majority of individual seeds. The average alone would have confirmed the result.

BenchmarkMF-DRO beforewith ROIchangeseed winsbest baselineverdict
Hartmann 6D7.995.93−2.054/5MF-MES 6.62beats it
Borehole 8D15.8211.59−4.221/5MF-MES 6.40still behind
Ackley 10D (abs.)3.833.74−0.091/5SF-DRO 3.43still behind
Currin 2D0.010.13+0.110/5MI-Greedy 0.00worse

What the calibration actually fixes. The paper defines the ROI as {x : UCB(x) ≥ max LCB} and leaves β unspecified, writing it as βt — with a subscript implying a schedule. The implementation used a constant. At a constant β, how much of the domain survives the filter is not a choice: it is whatever the posterior scale happens to produce, and it swings 250× within a single Borehole run (100% of the domain early, 0.4% late). Solving βt for a target acceptance instead makes tightness a knob. It also bounds the cost: a fixed β needs between 1 and 86 rejection passes over one run, and past a cap it silently dilutes the ROI back toward no filter at all.

Four reasons not to over-read this

One benchmark of four — and on a second the fix makes things worse. Borehole still loses by 5.2 points, Ackley by 0.31, and on Currin the ROI is actively harmful: 0.01 → 0.13, worse on every seed. The absolute damage there is small and Currin is effectively a solved problem for every method, but the direction is consistent. The calibrated ROI helps two benchmarks, does nothing on a third, and costs a little on the fourth.

Three ROI settings were tried on Hartmann and the winner reported. One of the other two is actively harmful (+1.56 points, worse than no ROI); the third is roughly neutral (−0.26). q=0.10 was not chosen on Hartmann — it also won Borehole — but a clean confirmation would fix it in advance and run fresh seeds. That confirmation is written and waiting on compute.

The bar was registered for a different configuration. Applying the original comparison’s threshold here is a post-hoc use of a pre-registered rule. The bar this experiment registered for itself failed.

n=5, no p-values, and 4/5 is a weak majority. This project has already retracted a 2/3 result that vanished at n=10.

Retraction · the high-fidelity floor

Announced, then withdrawn

Forcing at least one expensive evaluation in every window of four was proposed as a guard against a specific failure: on several Hartmann seeds the policy collapses to 94–96% cheap queries, taking only 6 to 12 expensive evaluations in an entire budget. On the first seed set it looked like it worked — the spread across seeds fell from 5.85 to 2.00 and the worst seed improved from 16.41 to 6.91. A clean re-test at five seeds never used before reversed every part of that.

seedno floorwith floordifferencelongest cheap-only run
522.54%2.54%+0.004
530.82%0.82%+0.001
540.76%9.07%+8.3011
555.78%5.45%−0.336
563.39%3.39%+0.001

The spread rose, 2.08 to 3.17. The average got worse by 1.60 points. One seed of five improved. The primary bar was variance reduction, chosen precisely because it was the robust half of the original result; it failed outright.

Worse than a null result. The collapse it was meant to fix does still happen at these seeds — cheap-only runs of 4, 11 and 6 — so the floor had something to act on. But the seed where the policy collapses hardest is the seed the floor damages most: seed 54 goes from 0.76% to 9.07%. Across the five, the correlation between how badly a run collapses and how much the floor helps is −0.84: the wrong sign. The explanation was not merely unconfirmed, it was backwards.

In hindsight the first seed set had cheap-only runs of 131, 73, 75 and 50 — far more extreme than anything here, where the worst is 11. Its control was unusually erratic, and most of the “spread reduction” was the floor reining in an unusually bad comparison rather than the floor being stabilising. The gain there came almost entirely from one seed, which was noted at the time and should have carried more weight than it did.

Two retractions, one shape

This is the second claim withdrawn here today. Both met their thresholds on five seeds, both were recorded as provisional with caveats attached, and both died when re-run on seeds that had never been used. The caveats were accurate and did not help. What separated the surviving results from these was re-running them, not judgement about which would hold.

The strongest result · n=10

One deficit is real, one is not

Both weak benchmarks were re-measured against the baseline on a second, independent set of five seeds. That doubles the evidence behind the table below, and it splits it in two.

BenchmarkseedsMF-DRObaselinemean gapmedian gapbaseline betterverdict
Hartmann 6D105.326.84−1.52+0.225/10no difference
Borehole 8D1015.428.24+7.18+8.308/10real deficit

Hartmann’s deficit is not real. Five wins of ten, median +0.22. The gap in the verdict table below was a property of the five seeds it was measured on, where MF-DRO scores 7.99; on the other five it scores 2.66.

Borehole’s is. The baseline wins eight of ten, and unlike Hartmann the median gap is larger than the mean — not one bad run dragging an average. It survives the change of seeds intact.

This matters for the two retractions above and for what survives them. The interventions were all developed on these two benchmarks, and Borehole is where the method genuinely loses — where the ROI helped most, where teacher refinement helped most (−2.11 points at fresh seeds, better on four of five, with its mechanism check independently passing), and where the boundary explanation applies. That work is aimed at something real.

But the diagnosis that opened this whole investigation was stated on Hartmann — “wastes 20.8% of its expensive budget” — and Hartmann is the benchmark whose deficit does not survive replication. On the second seed set the same configuration wastes 4.2%.

The finding that may outlast the rest

Five seeds cannot order two methods in this problem class. Four quantities measured during this work reverse or vanish when the seed set changes: a paired standard deviation (0.45 → 7.45), a tail-risk ordering, the incidence of the failure mode one intervention was built to fix (80% → 29%), and now the sign of a method comparison. Two benchmarks — Currin and Ackley — have still only ever been measured on the original five.

The runs

What the curves show

Diagnosis

It finds a good point. It wastes the budget getting there.

MF-MES shares MF-DRO’s KO surrogate, initial design and budget, so a difference between them isolates the policy. Scoring every high-fidelity query on (y − best_init) / (y_opt − best_init) — 1.0 is the optimum, 0.0 is no better than the starting design:

Benchmark · methodBest foundMean queryWorse than startHF queries
Hartmann · MF-DRO0.8580.33620.8%11.6
Hartmann · MF-MES0.8610.7475.3%22.0
Borehole · MF-DRO0.6330.3817.9%94.0
Borehole · MF-MES0.8520.6690.5%84.0

On Hartmann the two methods find the same best point — 0.858 against 0.861. What differs is everything else: MF-DRO’s average query is worth less than half as much, and one query in five lands worse than where it started. With only ~12 high-fidelity evaluations, roughly two and a half are spent going backwards.

The obvious explanation — that MF-DRO starves itself of high-fidelity evaluations — does not survive Borehole, where it makes more high-fidelity queries than MF-MES (94 vs 84) and still finds a worse maximum. Budget is not the binding constraint there.

The mechanism is the proposal step. MF-DRO runs its regression head, emitting x = action_head(h).clamp(0,1) directly with no acquisition maximisation at inference. Its training targets are rollout-teacher actions drawn from the candidate pool — which, with the ROI off, is uniform over the whole domain. The policy is trained on domain-spread targets and learns to propose diffusely: its per-dimension query spread is 3.5× MF-MES’s on Hartmann.

Correction

A conclusion on record was wrong

Borehole’s optimum sits on the domain boundary in 7 of 8 dimensions, and MF-DRO essentially never reaches those bounds. That hypothesis was investigated months ago and recorded as unsupported, because MF-DRO’s queries measured closest to the optimum of any method while having the worst regret — an inversion that appeared to kill it.

That refutation used unweighted Euclidean distance. Borehole’s output variance is almost entirely carried by four dimensions, and all four have boundary optima:

Dimx*Share of varianceMF-DRO reachesMF-MES reaches
01.0081.6%68%99%
60.008.0%2%70%
50.005.4%0%34%
31.004.6%1%49%
1, 2, 4, 7—0.4% total——

Weighting the distance by measured sensitivity reverses the comparison:

unweighted min d*   MF-DRO 0.2535  <  MF-MES 0.2998   ← the old refutation
weighted   min d*   MF-DRO 0.0543  >  MF-MES 0.0308   ← 76% farther

MF-DRO only looked closer because it sat nearer the optimum in the four dimensions carrying 0.4% of the variance. The inversion was an artifact of the metric. One link of the elimination chain is broken, and its conclusion — “surrogate hyperparameter constraints are what is left” — no longer follows. This is correlation plus a mechanism at n=5 on one benchmark, not causation.

The bug

Every previous ROI test was confounded

The DRO paper’s Region of Interest is the intended mechanism for focusing rollouts. It had been tried and abandoned. The rule itself turned out to be correct — it matches the paper and the single-fidelity implementation, is computed per ensemble member, and is held fixed across a rollout as the paper requires.

The defect was in the candidate pool. It filtered a fixed 2000-point draw, then padded back up to 600 with replacement. So switching the ROI on silently cut the number of distinct candidates:

Hartmann 6D, sqrt(beta)=2    ROI off:  600 distinct
                             ROI on:   231 distinct   ← 2.6x resolution cut

Turning the ROI on focused the region and cut resolution at the same moment, so harm attributed to the ROI could equally have come from the padding. Fixed by rejection-sampling to a fixed distinct count; the ROI-off path is gated bit-identical.

Also worth retiring

The recorded reason for deleting the ROI — “zero rollout steps within L2=0.2 of the optimum” — is reproduced by the unfiltered pool too: the closest of 2000 uniform points in 6 dimensions is 0.243 away. That is dimensionality, not the ROI.

Code audit · the deeper confound

The ROI has never been applied to a real query

This is not an experimental result. It is a fact about the execution path, found by reading it, and it reframes every ROI number on this page.

Turning the ROI on restricts the candidate pool that the teacher draws its demonstrations from, inside the rollout simulation that generates training data. The real query is a different code path entirely. It comes from one call, and with the candidate-scoring head off — the setting every experiment here used, because pool-and-argmax is excluded as a fix — that call returns:

x_t = self.action_head(h).clamp(0.0, 1.0)

Between that line and the query being issued, the only modifications are to fidelity — a cold-start override and the high-fidelity floor. No ROI symbol appears anywhere in the path.

So the ROI reaches a real query only by imitation: the teacher proposes inside the region, those proposals become the regression target, the head’s weights shift, and the emitted point drifts somewhat toward where the region was. The DRO paper defines the region as a constraint on where you query. What was implemented is a constraint on where the teacher demonstrates.

That is the best structural account available for the ROI’s signature — real but small on Borehole, negligible on Ackley, actively harmful on Currin, withdrawn on Hartmann. An intervention filtered through a lossy imitation channel should be weak and inconsistent across problems, which is exactly what was measured. It also fits the surrogate experiment: MF-DRO builds a better global model than the method that beats it, and fails to convert it into queries. The ROI aims at that conversion step, and then never touches it.

Three things this does not mean

It does not rescue anything. Both withdrawn results stay withdrawn. It does not predict the sign. A constraint that excludes the model’s preferred point can easily hurt — Currin is already harmed by the training-only version. It does not mean the imitation channel is inert. ROI-on and ROI-off runs really do differ; the question is how much, not whether.

The trap, named before walking toward it

“Enforce the region at inference” is one bad step from drawing candidates, keeping the ones inside, and picking the best by acquisition score — which is the pool-and-argmax mechanism that is excluded, because it would erase the contribution. The rule adopted: the region may say which points are admissible and may never rank them. If the model’s own output is admissible it is queried untouched; otherwise it is replaced by the nearest admissible point, by distance to that output. No acquisition function is evaluated.

That argument is not self-certifying, so the next experiment includes a control that snaps to an unfiltered pool. If the control explains the effect, then quantizing onto a finite pool did the work and the excluded mechanism resurfaced — and that is what will be reported, in those words.

The strategy

Calibrate the acceptance rate, solve for β

A constant β is unusable. Measured acceptance under the paper’s rule at sqrt(beta)=2, as high-fidelity data accumulates:

BenchmarkEarlyMidLate
Currin 2D20.0%8.0%1.7%
Hartmann 6D12.6%3.4%6.0%
Borehole 8D100.0%29.6%0.4%
Ackley 10D100.0%100.0%16.5%

A 250× swing on Borehole. The ROI is vacuous exactly when the surrogate is worst, then collapses to 8 points out of 2000 once data accumulates. Both are failure modes, in opposite directions, and neither is visible if you only check one benchmark at one stage.

So make the acceptance rate the controlled quantity and solve for βt by bisection. The ROI set stays exactly as the paper writes it; only the free parameter changes — and the paper writes β with a subscript t, implying a schedule, while the implementation used a constant. Acceptance is monotone in β, so bisection is valid. It hits a 10% target exactly on all four benchmarks, with βt spanning 0.31 to 12.29 — a 40× range no constant covers.

Before the results

What the mechanism checks predict

Both measurements below were run and committed before any h84 run completed, so they cannot be a post-hoc reading. Measuring the rollout teacher’s actions directly — the targets the policy regresses onto — at a matched model state on Hartmann:

ROIRefinementMean scoreBest score
off00.1730.974
off1000.2190.834
q = 0.1000.1830.717
q = 0.101000.2080.830

The ROI buys +0.010. Acquisition refinement buys +0.046, more than four times as much, and the two are not additive. Against the 0.336 → 0.747 gap the experiment is trying to close, +0.010 does not plausibly get there.

The ROI also costs reach: the single best teacher action falls from 0.974 to 0.717 when the ROI is switched on. Tightening it further, to q=0.02, moves the closest-ever approach to the optimum from 0.022 to 0.110 — the region containing the answer gets excluded. This is the failure the deleted implementation’s comment warned about; unlike that comment’s evidence, this version is a like-for-like test at matched resolution.

Registered prediction — and its refutation

On the evidence above I registered, twice and in writing before the runs, that the primary bar — a +0.10 improvement in mean query score on 4 of 5 seeds — was unlikely to be met.

That prediction is refuted on Borehole. With all five seeds complete, the quantile-calibrated ROI at q=0.10 gives +0.114 on mean query score, winning 5 of 5 seeds, and −4.22 points of relative regret, better on 5 of 5. Relative regret falls from 15.82% to 11.59%, and queries landing worse than the initial design fall from 7.9% to 3.0%.

The error is diagnosable rather than merely noted: I measured the ROI’s effect on the teacher’s action quality at a single model state and treated +0.010 as an upper bound on its effect on the policy. But the policy trains on the teacher’s whole action distribution across every rollout and iteration, and the ROI narrows that distribution — something a single-state mean cannot capture. A real measurement of the wrong quantity.

Two limits on that result, both load-bearing. Hartmann is far weaker (+0.039 at three of five seeds) and will likely miss the same bar, so the honest claim is that the strategy works on the benchmark it was aimed at and does not transfer at the same strength. And closing 45% of the gap does not make MF-DRO competitive: MF-MES still wins Borehole by 5.2 points, so the headline at the top of this page is unchanged.

The pattern underneath is the interesting part. On Borehole, tighter is better — q=0.10 (+0.114) beats q≈0.49 (+0.034) beats no ROI — and it tracks a monotone improvement in how often the method reaches the boundary where the optimum sits (sensitive-dimension hits 17.75% → 19.86% → 23.47%). On Hartmann, whose optimum is interior, the loose setting is if anything harmful. The best q is benchmark-dependent — which is expressible only because βt is solved for an acceptance rate, and unreachable with the fixed β the implementation shipped.

One genuine surprise sits alongside this. MF-DRO’s real queries score 0.336 while its teacher’s actions score 0.173–0.219 — the policy roughly doubles the average action it is trained on, which suggests the return-conditioning is doing real work rather than the policy merely imitating. The caveat is that those two numbers come from different model states, so only the ROI-versus-refinement contrast above is strictly like-for-like.

The one that survived

Teacher refinement, at a third of its first size

Three interventions were tried. Two were withdrawn above. The third survived a clean re-test — and shrank on the way through. Fixing how the rollout teacher searches for its next point (a local refinement around its broad pick, instead of a flat pick from random candidates) improved Borehole by 5.85 points on the first seed set. At five seeds never used before it is worth 2.11 points, better on four of five.

seedno refinementrefineddifference
5210.52%14.01%+3.49
5315.33%6.76%−8.57
5416.13%14.92%−1.21
5516.13%15.35%−0.79
5616.99%13.53%−3.46

The direction held; the size did not. A threshold set in advance required at least half the original effect, and 2.11 is 36% of it — so the earlier figure is corrected rather than repeated. Cost failed its registered bar: the limit was 2× the unmodified method, and refinement runs at 1.25× on these seeds but 2.07× on the original ones. The bar applies to the intervention, so one seed set exceeding it is a failure — the honest statement is that the cost is 1.25–2.07× depending on which seeds are drawn, not a single reassuring number. An earlier version of this page reported only the 1.25× figure and called it inside its limit.

It does not make the method competitive. Refined, MF-DRO reaches 12.91% on Borehole against the strongest baseline’s 10.07% at the same seeds. A prediction registered in advance said it would not close that gap. It did not.

One detail worth stating, because it nearly produced a false headline: these seeds are 3.67 points harder for the baseline than the original ones, while barely affecting MF-DRO. Had refinement reproduced its first size, MF-DRO would have appeared to overtake the baseline — on an accident of which seeds the baseline finds difficult. That reading was ruled out in writing before the runs finished.

Confirmation · Borehole

The one intervention that came back intact

Three interventions were tried. Re-tested on seeds they were never developed on, two were withdrawn outright and the third shrank by two thirds. This is the fourth such re-test, and the first where the result held.

seedwith ROIwithoutdifference
4711.56%17.60%−6.05
4813.79%15.67%−1.87
4910.54%14.52%−3.97
5013.11%18.88%−5.77
5112.27%12.05%+0.22

All three thresholds set in advance were met. Pooled over both seed sets the gain is 3.86 points, better on 9 of 10 seeds, and it kept 83% of the size it had on the seeds it was developed on. Teacher refinement kept 36%; the two withdrawn interventions kept nothing.

So the answer to the question this investigation started from is not negative. On this benchmark, the region-of-interest rule the paper itself defines — with its threshold recalibrated at every iteration instead of held at a constant — measurably stops the method wasting its expensive budget.

Why this one held, and it was decided in advance

The protocol gave a reason, before the runs, for expecting Borehole to hold where Hartmann failed. Hartmann’s gain came from one region setting out of three — the other two were neutral or harmful. Borehole’s appeared at all three settings tested, which makes it a property of applying a region at all rather than of the setting that happened to get picked. That distinction predicted both outcomes correctly.

The pre-registration is checkable rather than asserted. The scoring thresholds were committed at 18:54; the first result of any arm landed at 19:31 and the first treated run at 19:54 — 37 and 60 minutes later. A later amendment reorganised the script’s control flow, and the threshold expressions are byte-identical across that change.

It is also Borehole-only. The same region rule is negligible on Ackley, was withdrawn on Hartmann, and actively harms Currin. One benchmark improving is a finding about that benchmark until something explains why the other three do not.

The gain is in the bad runs, not the typical one

This part was not predicted in advance and is reported as such. The spread across seeds falls by 52% (standard deviation 2.67 to 1.28). Every other measure of spread — mean absolute deviation, interquartile range, range, standard error — gives 52% as well.

The improvement is concentrated where the method was worst, and more sharply than a summary statistic conveys: the worst seed improves by 5.77 points, while the best seed does not improve at all — it gets 0.22 worse. That is what removing bad outcomes looks like, rather than lifting the average, which is what the stated goal predicts.

Correction, same day

This paragraph first read “60% (2.37 to 0.96)” with the worst seed improving 5.40 and the best 1.51, and neither figure reproduces from the five values in the table above.

The worst/best pair was wrong outright. It compared the two arms’ extreme values, which come from different seeds, so it described an improvement that no single run made. The best seed does not improve at all. The corrected, paired figures are above, and the conclusion is slightly stronger for it.

The spread pair was a mismatched sample, not a mismatched statistic. 2.37 and 0.96 are both the standard deviation at the same ddof, computed over the pooled ten seeds rather than the five tabulated here: across ten seeds every measure of spread gives 60%, and across the five shown every measure gives 52%. An intermediate version of this note said a standard deviation had been compared against a mean absolute deviation. That diagnosis was wrong. It arose from a coincidence — the region arm’s five-seed mean absolute deviation is 0.963, almost exactly its ten-seed standard deviation of 0.960. The five-seed figures are quoted above so they can be checked against the table.

An earlier claim of lower tail risk was discarded during this investigation for comparing a method against a difference computed from it, which is negative by construction. This measurement is each arm’s own spread across seeds, which is the form that test has to take.

It still does not make the method competitive. With the region of interest it reaches 12.25% against the strongest baseline’s 6.40%. That closes 37% of the gap (9.34 points down to 5.85), not half of it — and a prediction registered before the runs said the gap would not close.

One caveat that belongs next to that comparison and was missing from it: the baseline’s 6.40% was measured on the development seeds, while 12.25% is on the fresh ones, and this investigation has already found the same benchmark to differ by up to 3.67 points between seed sets. The two numbers are not strictly comparable, and settling it means re-running the baseline on seeds 47–51.

Status

What is running and what is open

  • The Borehole confirmation is complete and is reported above. At three of five pairs it was running weaker and was not unanimous; the analysis script refuses to print a verdict below five pairs, and none was read until all five were in. The final result met every threshold. The same run supplies teacher refinement with a third independent seed set, still in flight.
  • The next experiment is written and deliberately not launched. It applies the region of interest to the query rather than to the teacher — the version the paper actually defines. Its implementation is held outside the source tree as a patch, because another session has workers running and jobs still to launch, and a newly started worker would import an edited file mid-experiment. Its bit-identity check has not been run; no result from it may be reported until that passes.
  • Its primary prediction is registered as genuinely uncertain, which is a change of posture rather than a hedge. Eight mechanism claims have been registered in this investigation and seven were refuted. The one that held was the only one derived from a measurement taken before the claim was made.
  • Two baselines under-optimise on Ackley and Hartmann — MI-Greedy and MF-GP-UCB beat their own initial design between 0.8 and 3.0 times out of 20–40 high-fidelity queries. Cause unresolved; the leading candidate is the reference implementation’s deliberately inflated prior mean.
  • The boundary finding has no causal test. Changing the head’s output parameterisation and re-measuring Borehole is the experiment that would settle it.

A correction to this page’s own record-keeping

Earlier today I reported that a concurrent session had breached the compute limit — 27 workers on 15 cores. It had not. There were fifteen. The launcher process carries every queued job name in its arguments, and the script I wrote to count workers attributed that one process many times over. The load average was consistent with fifteen and I did not reconcile it before reporting. The counter has been fixed to exclude launchers.

All figures regenerated from the 100 h83 runs. Simple regret is recomputed from each run’s recorded query trace and cross-checked against every optimizer’s own final value to 1e−6; a mismatch is treated as a hard failure. No p-values are reported at n=5.
